newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, lawmakers meet on Medicare legislation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, lawmakers meet on Medicare legislation.

text.p: President Clinton discussed pending Medicare reform legislation with congressional health care policy power-brokers Tuesday and the White House said the meeting on how to economise on the programme was a positive one.

Under a balanced-budget agreement reached by Clinton and Congress, lawmakers must craft legislation to cut spending on the government health insurance plan for the elderly by $115 billion over five years.
"There really was a sense in the room that we can get this done despite the disagreements that exist on some issues," White House spokesman Barry Toiv told reporters afterwards.

The Republican proposal, largely modelled on the budget agreement, includes a slight increase in Medicare premiums. The bulk of savings -- roughly $100 billion -- would come from cutting payments to doctors, hospitals and managed care plans.
The plan also provides for tax-free medical savings accounts (MSAs), which the White House claims would undermine the medical insurance programme for the elderly.

Under the plan, Medicare recipients who opted for MSAs would be given a set amount of money to be deposited in a tax-free savings account. Funds could be withdrawn for routine medical bills and money left over at the end of the year could be rolled over to the next.

Republicans say the proposal would make seniors more cost-conscious health shoppers. The administration fears the youngest, healthiest Medicare recipients will opt for the plan -- leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular Medicare programme and increasing costs.

Representative Fortney Stark, a California Democrat who took part in the meeting, said Clinton and the lawmakers talked about the possible expansion of an existing pilot programme and said this "may be the genesis of a compromise."
"It would give us time to design it (a permanent program), and I think that's one of the big questions -- how it would work," he said.

Stark said the meeting focused on "finding a way to get this very good start of a health care bill to the (House) floor and passed." A House Ways and Means subcommittee is expected to approve the bill this week.
